noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand how the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries relate to their function

primer.text: Blood reaches every corner of you through three kinds of pipe, each built for a different pressure and job. Arteries fire blood outward at full force, veins gather it gently home, and capillaries trade substances with every tissue in between. Learn which wall fits which workload.

lessons.title: Arteries and Veins Under Pressure
lessons.opening: Arteries push blood outward at high pressure through thick, elastic walls and a narrow lumen, while veins return it at low pressure through thin walls, a wide bore and one-way valves.
keyPoints: Arteries leave the heart carrying oxygenated blood, except the pulmonary artery.
Thick muscular walls with elastic fibres withstand and maintain high pressure.
A narrow lumen helps arteries hold their pressure.
Veins run low-pressure and deoxygenated, except the pulmonary vein.
Valves inside veins stop the blood flowing backwards.

low.restatement: Arteries: thick, narrow, high pressure, outward. Veins: thin, wide, low pressure, homeward with valves.
low.analogy: A pressure hose versus a lazy river: one blasts, one drifts with gates to stop backflow.
low.examPointer: Learn the two exceptions cold: pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated, pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

medium.restatement: Wall thickness tracks pressure: elastic recoil keeps arterial flow surging forward, while venous valves make up for the missing push.
medium.analogy: A reinforced garden hose for the jet, and a wide lazy canal with lock gates for the return trip.
medium.examPointer: Structure-function questions want the pairing stated twice: feature, then the consequence for flow.

check.stem: Which direction do arteries carry blood?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That is the veins' direction.
Pulmonary vessels are just two members of the arterial set.
Blood runs heart-to-organs or organs-to-heart, never sideways.

check.stem: Why do arteries have thick muscular walls with elastic fibres?

options.text: To withstand the high pressure and recoil to maintain it as blood passes
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: To absorb oxygen from the blood
options.explanation: Gas exchange never happens in vessel walls.
Arterial flow is fast, not slowed.
The walls manage pressure, not storage.

check.stem: Which vessel is the exception that carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The aorta carries oxygenated blood to the body.
That vein returns deoxygenated blood toward the heart.
It carries oxygenated blood toward the heart.

check.stem: What do valves inside veins achieve?

options.text: They prevent backflow of the low-pressure blood
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Veins cannot pump; the heart and muscles move venous blood.
Valves direct flow; they do not pressurise.
Filtering is a kidney and liver job.

check.stem: Why does a vein's large lumen suit its job?

options.text: It reduces resistance to flow under low pressure
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It raises the pressure to heart levels
options.explanation: Veins run low-pressure by design.
Lumen width is the bore, not the wall.

options.text: It traps oxygen for the tissues
options.explanation: No trapping happens in any vessel.

check.stem: State three structural differences between arteries and veins.
check.modelAnswer: Arteries have thick muscular walls, narrow lumens and no valves; veins have thin walls, large lumens and valves.

check.stem: Name the two exceptions to the usual oxygen content of arteries and veins.
check.modelAnswer: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

check.stem: Explain why elastic recoil in artery walls matters for steady blood delivery.
check.modelAnswer: The walls stretch during each pulse and then recoil, smoothing the surge and keeping the pressure up between heartbeats, so flow continues steadily.

check.stem: A nurse finds a patient's leg veins swollen with pooled blood. Link the finding to a valve problem.
check.modelAnswer: Faulty valves let venous blood run backwards, so it pools in the low-pressure leg veins instead of riding toward the heart.

lessons.title: Capillaries, the Exchange Vessels
lessons.opening: Capillaries thread through every tissue as one-cell-thick tubes whose leaky walls let plasma escape into the spaces around cells, making them the exchange points where substances actually pass between blood and tissue.
keyPoints: Capillary walls are a single cell thick, so diffusion distances stay short.
Their leaky walls let plasma seep out and form tissue fluid.
They run at low pressure inside the tissues.
They carry both oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Exchange of substances happens across their thin walls.

low.restatement: Thin, leaky, slow — capillaries are built for trading substances, not for speed.
low.analogy: Market stalls: the road narrows and slows so buyers and sellers can actually trade.
low.examPointer: Say 'one cell thick' exactly; 'very thin' earns less in mark schemes.

medium.restatement: Short diffusion distance plus leaking plasma combine to deliver oxygen and nutrients while collecting wastes efficiently.
medium.analogy: A drive-through window at walking pace: close enough to pass goods either way.
medium.examPointer: Mention tissue fluid by name when explaining the leaky walls; it is the term examiners look for.

check.stem: How thick is a capillary wall?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Several cells thick like a vein
options.explanation: Vein walls are layered; capillary walls are not.
Capillaries are the thinnest of the three.

options.text: It has no wall at all
options.explanation: A wall exists, just extremely thin.

check.stem: What does the leakiness of capillary walls achieve?

options.text: Plasma escapes to form tissue fluid around the cells
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Pressure is low in capillaries.
Cells stay inside; only plasma leaks.
Capillaries have no valves.

check.stem: Why does the one-cell-thick wall suit exchange?

options.text: It gives a very short diffusion distance for substances
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Capillaries run at low pressure.
Temperature is irrelevant to the wall's role.
Leakage is precisely the design.

options.text: Both oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, as exchange proceeds along their length
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
They lose oxygen to the tissues as they run.
They start oxygenated at the arterial end.
Blood cells and plasma both flow through.

check.stem: At what speed does blood move through capillaries?

options.text: Slowly, giving exchange time to happen
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Arteries are the fast lanes; capillaries crawl.
Blood flows, just slowly.
The aorta flow far outpaces capillary flow.

check.stem: State the role of capillaries in the circulatory system.
check.modelAnswer: They exchange substances with the tissues across thin, leaky walls at low pressure.

check.stem: Name the fluid that leaks from capillaries to surround cells.
check.modelAnswer: Tissue fluid forms when plasma leaks out of capillaries.

check.stem: Explain why the slow capillary flow rate is an advantage.
check.modelAnswer: Slower passage gives more time for diffusion, so oxygen and nutrients leave and wastes enter across the thin wall before the blood moves on.

check.stem: An athlete's muscles need more glucose during a race. Describe how the capillaries serve that demand.
check.modelAnswer: Capillaries widen their network in active muscle, and their thin leaky walls deliver glucose and oxygen into the tissue fluid quickly while carrying carbon dioxide away.

glossary.definition: A vessel carrying blood at high pressure away from the heart.
A low-pressure vessel returning blood toward the heart, fitted with valves.
A one-cell-thick exchange vessel running through the tissues.
Plasma that has leaked out of capillaries to bathe the cells.
